title: Why the Gradient Is Steepest: A Cosine of Heading
topic: At a point, the directional derivative in unit heading u is D_u f = grad f . u = |grad f| cos(theta), where theta is the angle between u and the gradient. As the heading rotates a full turn, the climb rate traces a cosine: maximum when u aligns with the gradient (steepest ascent), zero when perpendicular (along the level curve), minimum when opposite (steepest descent). That is why the gradient is the direction of fastest increase.

beats.narration: From one spot on a hill you can step in any direction. Which heading climbs the fastest?

elements.content: Every heading has a climb rate — which is biggest?

beats.narration: The gradient is one fixed arrow. Pick a heading u; the climb rate is the gradient dotted with u — which is the gradient's length times the cosine of the angle between them.

elements.content: Point P with fixed gradient arrow ∇f (amber) and a heading u (teal); dashed level-curve direction
θ is the angle from the gradient to your heading.

beats.narration: Turn the heading all the way around. The climb rate traces a cosine — highest when you face along the gradient, and it sinks from there.

elements.content: Heading u rotates 360° around P; angle arc θ from the gradient
Response plot D_u f vs θ traced in sync as u rotates, amber cosine
Marker on the cosine tracking the current heading

beats.narration: Straight along the gradient is steepest ascent. Ninety degrees off, you are walking the level curve and the rate is zero. Turn fully around and you get the steepest descent.

elements.content: Full cosine with three marks: max (ascent), zero (along contour), min (descent)

beats.narration: So the gradient is not just perpendicular to the contour — it is the single heading of fastest climb.

elements.content: 'The gradient is the heading of fastest climb.' serif italic
Every other heading is just a cosine slice of it.
